rows.speaker: أبو الضحى
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits an interrupted report that the Quraysh had 360 idols around the Kaaba; on hearing the verse they demanded a recognizable proof, and it was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: فلما سمعوا هذه الآية تعجبوا وقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the polytheists' extreme ignorance kept them from accepting the comprehensive proof already implied by the verse's two descriptions.
rows.anchor: ولفرط جهلهم لم يكفهم الحجة الإجمالية المشير إليها الوصفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens are plural because people benefit from all their parts, including starlight, whereas the earth is singular because only the one earth they observe benefits them.
rows.anchor: وإنما جمع ( السموات ) وأفرد ( الأرض ) للإنتفاع بجميع أجزاء الأولى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says earth is not pluralized because the plural is heavy and would oppose the pattern; some singulars have no Qurʾanic plural and some plurals no singular.
rows.anchor: لأن جمعها ثقيل وهو مخالف للقياس

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: A scholarly view says the seven heavens are distinct personal layers, whether touching as philosophers hold or separated by journeys of five hundred years in reports; differences in their effects indicate different natures.
rows.anchor: لأنها طبقات ممتازة كل واحدة من الأخرى بذاتها الشخصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day may mean their alternation, each succeeding the other, or their internal variation in length, increase and decrease, darkness and light.
rows.anchor: أي تعاقبهما وكون كل منهما خلفا للآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is mentioned before day either because it was created first or because it is more noble.
rows.anchor: لسبقه في الخلق أو لشرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about ships is coordinated either with the creation of the heavens or with night and day, not with the word heavens alone.
rows.anchor: عطف على ( خلق السموات ) لا على ( السموات )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulk is used for both singular and plural; its vowel may be original as in qufl or incidental as in asad, and the syntax can reveal number.
rows.anchor: تغاير اعتباري فإن أعتبر أن ضمته أصلية

rows.speaker: الكواشي
rows.claim: Al-Kawāshī says fulk and fulk with two ḍammas are dialect forms whose written form is the same in singular and plural, distinguished by verb-pronoun agreement.
rows.anchor: وقال الكواشي : الفلك والفلك بضمتين لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In bimā yanfaʿu al-nās, mā can be a verbal noun, meaning by their benefiting people, or a relative pronoun, meaning what benefits them; a descriptive mā poorly fits the argument.
rows.anchor: إما مصدرية أي بنفعهما وموصولة أي بالذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun with the verbal-noun reading may refer to the ship (masculine in form, feminine in meaning), its sailing, or the sea.
rows.anchor: ضمير الفاعل إما للفلك لأنه مذكر اللفظ مؤنث المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain clause is coordinated with ships; its later placement despite its broader benefit may give it extra emphasis, while another account explains the ship mention as a route to knowledge of the sea's wonders.
rows.anchor: قيل : وتأخيره عن ذكرها مع كونه أعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the proposal that the sea, rather than ships, is the actual object of inference: it reverses the revealed order without evidence, and ships themselves display divine ordering.
rows.anchor: وعندي أن هذا خلاف الظاهر جدا وإن جل قائله إذ يؤول المعنى إلى والبحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ships can themselves be signs through their changing courses, heavy cargo, and buoyancy amid waves despite the air's delicacy and their own weight; their travel serves human livelihood.
rows.anchor: وأي مانع من كون الاستدلال باختلاف الفلك وذهابها مرة كذا ومرة كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order first pairs upper and lower creation, then phenomena shaped by heaven and earth, then ships moving in the sea; rain follows as a sign linking the upper and lower worlds and benefiting people.
rows.anchor: ذكر أولا خلق أمرين علوي وسفلي واختلاف شيئين بمدخلية أمرين سماوي وأرضي ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night, sun, moon, and ship passages are compared with the signs in another verse; there the night/day signs explicitly mediate between ship and its mention, whereas this verse first hints at them and then turns to rain.
rows.anchor: نسلخ منه النهار فإذا هم مظلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two occurrences of min are read first as indicating origin and then as explanatory; min al-samāʾ means the direction above, though other grammatical parses are possible.
rows.anchor: والثانية بيانية وجوز أن تكون تبعيضية وأن تكون بدلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revives the earth by stirring its latent growth and bringing forth plants, flowers, and trees after dryness has suppressed their appearance.
rows.anchor: بتهييج قواها النامية وإظهار ما أودع فيها من أنواع النبات والأزهار والأشجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about spreading creatures may coordinate with sending down water as an independent sign sharing God's agency, or with reviving earth as a consequence of the water; on the latter parse, water sustains animals and their spread follows life.
rows.anchor: والجامع كون كل منهما آية مستقلة لوحدانيته تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min kulli dābbah is explanatory of the kinds of creatures that crawl on earth; their multiplication by birth or generation is evidence because every kind is represented, not just some kinds.
rows.anchor: على التقدير الأول على الصحيح والمراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A partitive reading is proposed because not every possible individual was created, but al-Ālūsī objects that partitive min denotes a portion of its complement, not one individual of a kind; heavenly creatures do not undermine the earthly reading.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن بث كل نوع مما يدب على الأرض لا ينافي كون بعض أفراده مقدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's turning of winds includes directions, warm and cold, violent and gentle, barren and fecund, and winds of mercy or punishment.
rows.anchor: أي تقليب الله تعالى لها جنوبا وشمالا وقبولا ودبورا حارة وباردة

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the noun in the singular, with الريح understood generically; Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes plural winds of mercy from singular wind of punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي الريح على الأفراد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed when wind blew: asking that it be winds of mercy and not a wind of punishment; al-Ālūsī relates this to the cited scriptural usages.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم كان إذا هبت ريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds follow the revived earth and creatures because they nourish plants and preserve animal life; some reports say that if God withheld wind for an hour, everything between heaven and earth would stink.
rows.anchor: وعقب إحياء الأرض بالمطر وبث كل دابة فيها بتصريف الرياح لأن في ذلك تربية النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sahāb is a collective noun, with sahābah as its singular; the name may derive from its drifting through the air or from winds drawing it along.
rows.anchor: وهو اسم جنس واحده سحابة سمي بذلك لانسحابه في الجو أو لجر الرياح له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-musakhkhar is an adjective for cloud, matching its grammatical form or its collective meaning; bayna is an adjunct, or a circumstantial phrase with an omitted complement about winds turning the cloud by God's will.
rows.anchor: وقد يعتبر معناه فيوصف بالجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cloud's subjection means it neither falls nor vanishes, although its lightness would naturally lift it and its density would make it descend; another parse makes it subject to winds that turn it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى تسخيره أنه لا ينزل ولا يزول مع أن الطبع يقتضي صعوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cloud follows wind because it is like the wind's effect and because ending with a heavenly sign echoes the opening's upper-and-lower ordering.
rows.anchor: وتعقيت تصريف الرياح بالسحاب لأنه كالمعلول للرياح

rows.speaker: بعض الفضلاء
rows.claim: One scholar says wind and cloud come last despite their natural order to stress that each listed phenomenon is an independent sign; al-Ālūsī doubts that anyone would otherwise mistake them for one sign.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الفضلاء : لعل تأخير تصريف الرياح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delayed predicate of inna bears the emphatic lām, and its indefinite form magnifies the signs in both number and greatness: they attest overwhelming power, wisdom, and mercy, warranting exclusive worship.
rows.anchor: لتأخره عن خبرها والتنكير للتفخيم كما وكيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿqilūn uses reason figuratively for reflection, the fruit of reason; a report from ʿĀʾishah says the Prophet warned readers who recite the verse without reflecting.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها أن النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contingent things take one determinate form among possibilities and entail specific effects, so they require a chooser who is powerful, knowing, and wise; this reasoning also reproaches the polytheists' demand for another sign.
rows.anchor: كل واحد من هذه الأمور المعدودة قد وجد على وجه خاص من الوجوه الممكنة دون ما عداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two independent gods would either jointly cause one effect, leave one without a reason to be preferred, or oppose each other's different intentions; every case entails incapacity, incompatible with divinity.
rows.anchor: إذ لو كان معه واجب يقدر على ما يقدر الحق تعالى عليه فإن وافقت إرادة كل منهما إيجاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports rational proof, the nobility of kalām and its scholars, and perhaps the discipline of astronomy.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية إثبات الاستدلال بالحجج العقلية وتنبيه على شرف علم الكلام وفضل أهله

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: A report from Kaʿb ibn Mālik says that Ramadan rules once prohibited food, drink, and sex after sleeping; ʿUmar and Kaʿb each approached a sleeping wife, then ʿUmar told the Prophet and this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن كعب بن مالك قال : كان الناس في رمضان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Ibn ʿAbbās's account, ʿUmar confessed to the Prophet after his sleeping self prompted intercourse; God then sent an allowance in a Qurʾanic verse and ordered its placement in the middle hundred verses of al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما بينما هو نائم إذ سولت له نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylat al-ṣiyām means the night before the day one fasts; the genitive is a loose association, and the phrase is generic. Rafath may govern it or be governed by an omitted word, or it may be an adverb of uhilla.
rows.anchor: الليلة التي يصبح منها صائما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rafath can mean obscene speech, but here it means intercourse, which commonly entails explicit speech; the verb's preposition reflects an incorporated sense of intimate approach.
rows.anchor: أفحش وأفصح بما يكنى عنه والمراد به هنا الجماع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, challenged about rafath while in ihram, said it means what occurs with women; his quoted verse can describe speech or conduct.
rows.anchor: فقيل له : أرفثت فقال : إنما الرفث ما كان عند النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit term is chosen instead of Qurʾanic euphemisms such as touching and entering because the point is intercourse itself and the wording rebukes their earlier conduct, later called betrayal.
rows.anchor: ولم يجعل من أول الأمر كناية عنه لأن المقصود هو الجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women is a plural of niswah or a non-form-based plural of imraʾah; the possessive marks the marital or owned relationship that makes intimacy lawful.
rows.anchor: والنساء جمع نسوة فهو جمع الجمع أو جمع امرأة على غير اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh has rafūth; the garment metaphor means spouses are repose for one another, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, or that they embrace and cover/protect one another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله الرفوث هن لباس لكم وأنتم لباس لهن أي هن سكن لكم وأنتم سكن لهن قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās supports the garment metaphor with a verse by al-Nābighah describing a lover's embrace as a garment.
rows.anchor: وأنشد رضي الله تعالى عنهما لما قال له هل تعرف العرب ذلك قول الذبياني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two garment clauses are grammatically independent, not an explanatory rhetorical supplement; they explain the ruling by the spouses' little patience and difficulty avoiding one another, with the man's need placed first.
rows.anchor: والجملتان مستأنفتان استئنافا نحويا والبياني يأباه الذوق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: An unattributed report says there is no good in women and no patience without them; the honorable person may be overcome by them, which the quoted speaker prefers to being a base victor.
rows.anchor: وفي الخبر لا خير في النساء ولا صبر عنهن يغلبن كريما ويغلبهن لئيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here God's knowing means the attachment of His knowledge; ikhtiyān is either desire inclining a person to betrayal or intensive betrayal that diminishes the self and exposes it to punishment.
rows.anchor: الخيانة البليغة فيكون تنقصون أنفسكم تنقيصا تاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past and imperfect forms indicate that the people had persisted in the forbidden conduct before being informed of the allowance; the past-tense sequence conflicts with an eternal-knowledge interpretation adopted by some.
rows.anchor: والمراد الاستمرار عليه فيما مضى قبل إخبارهم بالحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's turning toward them follows their repentance; one interpretation distinguishes removal of the prohibition from forgiveness of the sin, while the two clauses may otherwise overlap.
rows.anchor: والمراد قبل توبتكم حين تبتم عن المحظور الذي ارتكبتموه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes al-ān as the time when the ban on intercourse is lifted, linked to the dawn limit; it may also denote the near future as present or be literal with an implied 'We have permitted.'
rows.anchor: نظرا إلى ما هو المقصود من الإحلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubāsharah literally means skin touching skin and is idiomatic for intercourse because intercourse entails it.
rows.anchor: وأصل المباشرة إلزاق البشرة بالبشرة وأطلقت على الجماع للزومها لها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and others interpret 'what God wrote for you' as children decreed in the heavenly record; the command means praying for them despite not knowing one's decree.
rows.anchor: وهو المروي عن ابن عباس والضحاك ومجاهد رضي الله تعالى عنهم وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse teaches that intercourse should seek preservation of human offspring, not merely satisfaction, just as appetite for food preserves individuals; pleasure alone suits beasts.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على أن المباشر ينبغي أن يتحرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read 'what God wrote' as a prohibition of withdrawal or anal intercourse; others take it as seeking the prescribed ejaculation in its proper place, excluding those acts. The author notes juristic differences about consent to withdrawal.
rows.anchor: وجعل بعضهم هذا الطلب كناية عن النهي عن العزل أو عن إتيان المحاش

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reportedly interprets 'what God wrote' as Laylat al-Qadr; the same interpretation is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وروى عن أنس رضي الله تعالى عنه تفسير ذلك بليلة القدر وحكي عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنه أيضا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah interprets the command as seeking the concession God prescribed, since God loves that His concessions be accepted as His strict duties are; this reinforces the preceding permission.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أن المراد ( ابتغوا ) الرخصة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: When ʿAṭāʾ asked Ibn ʿAbbās whether the reading is ibtaghū or attabiʿū, Ibn ʿAbbās allowed either but advised the first reading.
rows.anchor: وعن عطاء أنه سئل ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما كيف تقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The white thread is the first horizontal light of true dawn; the black thread is the remaining night darkness alongside it. Taking it as the false vertical dawn is an error.
rows.anchor: وهو أول ما يبدو من الفجر الصادق المعترض في الأفق قبل انتشاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take min al-fajr as explaining the white thread alone, from which the black thread is understood; others explain both threads because dawn can encompass them, citing a poetic image of blue dawn preceding its white light.
rows.anchor: على أن ( الفجر ) عبارة عن مجموعهما لقول الطائي

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl ibn Saʿd reports that some tied actual white and black threads to their legs and kept eating until the words 'from dawn' were revealed; al-Ālūsī says this does not prove the earlier wording was unintelligible or that explanation was delayed past need.
rows.anchor: عن سهل بن سعد رضي الله تعالى عنهما قال : أنزلت

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim says he placed a black cord and white cord under his pillow, could not distinguish them, and reported the mistake to the Prophet in the morning.
rows.anchor: عن عدي بن حاتم رضي الله تعالى عنه قال : لما أنزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once dawn is specified, the thread imagery functions as a simile rather than a sustained metaphor; min may be partitive because the first visible light is part of dawn.
rows.anchor: لأن شرطها عندهم تناسيه بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first min is better attached to yatabayyan with the sense 'be distinguished': dawn must be separated from night haze; saying only 'dawn becomes clear' leaves multiple degrees and an unclear endpoint.
rows.anchor: إباحة ما تقدم ( حتى يتبين ) أحدهما من الآخر ويميز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that the verse was revealed before Ramadan in an ambiguous form requiring delayed explanation is criticized: explanation may follow the address only if it does not miss the time of need.
rows.anchor: وهي مبهمة والبيان ضروري إلا أنه تأخر عن وقت الخطاب

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls the addition 'from dawn' abrogation because Companions acted on the apparent wording and it then became figurative; al-Ālūsī objects that abrogation requires independent speech.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : إن هذا من باب النسخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the earlier bans on intercourse, eating, and drinking came from Prophetic practice, the verse shows Scripture abrogating Sunna; the 'made lawful' wording supports this, though abrogation without a replacement is disputed.
rows.anchor: دليل على جواز نسخ السنة بالكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permission to have intercourse until dawn supports a valid fast begun while junub, since a person could be made junub at the last moment of night; some reject this argument based on contrary reports.
rows.anchor: واستدل بالآية على صحة صوم الجنب لأنه يلزم من إباحة المباشرة إلى تبين الفجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Emission after dawn from intercourse begun before it does not defeat the argument: the emission completes intercourse in daytime, whereas junub status is a necessary consequence of the nighttime act.
rows.anchor: ولا يرد خروج المني بعد الصبح بالجماع الحاصل قبله لأنه إنما يفسد الصوم لكونه مكمل الجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also permits eating while one is unsure whether dawn has arrived, because the limit is the dawn's becoming clear; some jurists disagree about making up the fast if dawn had in fact begun.
rows.anchor: على جواز الأكل مثلا لمن شك في طلوع الفجر

rows.speaker: سعيد بن منصور
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr transmits a similar view that no makeup is required when a person ate under uncertainty, but al-Ālūsī says this is not the stronger position.
rows.anchor: وليس بالمنصور والأئمة الأربعة

rows.speaker: الأئمة الأربعة
rows.claim: The four imams hold that the legal day starts at true dawn, making prohibited acts forbidden after it; al-Aʿmash instead starts it at sunrise, as do the Imāmīs, interpreting min as partitive and dawn as the final portion of night.
rows.anchor: والأئمة الأربعة رضي الله تعالى عنهم

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash argues that day begins at sunrise, citing a report that daytime prayer is silent and analogizing the dawn light before sunrise to evening light after sunset; al-Ālūsī replies that the report may use day colloquially.
rows.anchor: وخالف في ذلك الأعمش ولا يتبعه إلا الأعمى فزعم أن أوله طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim mistook the threads for literal cords, the Prophet said his pillow must be broad: the white and black mean daylight and night-darkness.
rows.anchor: إنما ذاك بياض النهار من سواد الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Until night is attached to completing the fast, or is a circumstantial phrase; it cannot be the limit of the obligation itself because the obligation is not temporally extended. Either reading excludes night from fasting and joining two days into one fast.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون حالا من الصيام فيتعلق بمحذوف ولا يجوز جعله غاية للإيجاب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is said to have inferred the prohibition of continuous fasting from the command to finish at night; Laylā, wife of Bashīr ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyyah, recounts that her husband stopped her two-day fast and relayed the Prophet's warning against imitating Christians.
rows.anchor: إن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم نهى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not require an intervening meal before another fast, despite a claim to that effect; it directs people to break when night arrives.
rows.anchor: ولا تدل الآية على أنه لا يجوز الصوم حتى يتخل الإفطار خلافا لزاعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that then complete the fast, coordinated with the earlier night commands, can allow intention during the day: the definite fast refers to the already described abstention, commanded after dawn and after the night has ended.
rows.anchor: للعهد على ما هو الأصل فيكون مفاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because strict daytime intention from the verse and nighttime intention from the hadith cannot both be mandatory, consensus permits daytime intention for Ramadan, preserving both proofs; otherwise one would be discarded.
rows.anchor: فقلنا بالجواز عملا بهما فإن قيل :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that a Qurʾanic command to complete the fast should defeat a solitary report is answered by noting that the verse's apparent force has already been qualified by consensus, leaving room for the report to explain it.
rows.anchor: أجيب بأنها متروكة الظاهر بالإجماع فلم تبق قاطعة فيجوز أن يكون الخبر بيانا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another Shāfiʿī argument for obligatory nighttime intention is rejected as unsupported; no fasting obligation begins before dawn that could require prior intention.
rows.anchor: ولبعض الأصحاب تقرير الاستدلال بوجه آخر ولعل ما ذكرناه أقل مؤنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿtikāf linguistically means confinement or staying; in law it is a specified period of residence, and the passage forbids intercourse with a spouse during it.
rows.anchor: اللغة الاحتباس واللزوم مطلقا ومنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intercourse prohibition does not itself settle whether touching or kissing is forbidden: they may be allowed without desire or prohibited with desire, with a Shāfiʿī majority holding invalidation in that case; the broader skin-contact reading conflicts with ʿĀʾishah's grooming report.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه لزم من إباحة الجماع إباحة اللمس والقبلة وغيرهما بخلاف النهي

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah used to comb the Prophet's head while he was in iʿtikāf, a report against construing mubāsharah here as any skin contact.
rows.anchor: كانت عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها ترجل رأس النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning mosques as the setting for iʿtikāf indicates that it is valid only in a mosque; otherwise a home would count, contrary to consensus.
rows.anchor: دليل على أنه لا يصح إلا في المسجد

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: The juristic reports restrict iʿtikāf to a congregational mosque according to al-Zuhrī, a mosque with a regular imam and muezzin according to Abū Ḥanīfah, and the three mosques according to Ḥudhayfah.
rows.anchor: ويختص بالمسجد الجامع عند الزهري

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Further restrictions are attributed to ʿAlī (the Sacred Mosque only) and Ibn al-Musayyib (that mosque or the Prophet's Mosque); al-Shāfiʿī allows every mosque because the wording is unrestricted.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه لا يجوز إلا في المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: نافع مولى ابن عمر
rows.claim: Some infer that women may perform iʿtikāf outside mosques because women are not included in the masculine address, and that fasting is a condition and the minimum stay is a day; this is attributed to Nāfiʿ and ʿĀʾishah.
rows.anchor: على صحة اعتكاف المرأة في غير المسجد

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī requires neither a day nor fasting for iʿtikāf, citing a sound report from Ibn ʿAbbās that fasting is not required unless the worshipper imposes it on himself; similar reports are attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and two versions from ʿAlī differ.
rows.anchor: والشافعي رضي الله تعالى عنه لا يشترط يوما ولا صوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some infer intercourse invalidates iʿtikāf because a prohibition in worship entails invalidity, al-Ālūsī distinguishes an act prohibited within the ritual from a prohibited act merely coinciding with it.
rows.anchor: وهو ليس من العبادات لا يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six preceding rulings are called God's boundaries, barriers between right and wrong; 'do not approach them' figuratively commands avoiding falsehood and is stronger than simply forbidding transgression.
rows.anchor: أي حاجزة بين الحق والباطل

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim interprets 'do not approach them' as not altering the rulings, like the prohibition on approaching an orphan's property; al-Ālūsī says this and other alternatives strain the wording.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم : معنى ( لا تقربوها ) لا تتعرضوا لها بالتغيير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects an interpretation that treats the rulings as forbidden for others to legislate or as a boundary between divinity and servitude, calling it far from the intended sense.
rows.anchor: وهو بعيد بمراحل عن المقصود كما لا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's explanation of signs repeats the explanation given for fasting, or extends to all legal signs, so people may avoid disobeying commands and prohibitions; the parenthetical placement urges observance.
rows.anchor: كذلك أي مثل ذلك التبيين الواقع في أحكام الصوم يبين الله آياته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After fasting, the text turns to forbidding unlawful consumption, which could undermine acceptance of fasting and iʿtikāf.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر سبحانه الصيام وما فيه عقبه بالنهي عن الأكل الحرام المفضي إلى عدم قبول عبادته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah reports that men used to leave iʿtikāf to have intercourse with their wives and return, after which they were forbidden to do so.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده ما روى عن قتادة كان الرجل يعتكف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inference that leaving the mosque permits intercourse outside it is answered by reading the rule as applying while one remains legally an iʿtikāf participant; leaving for a need does not end iʿtikāf.
rows.anchor: ومن خرج من المسجد لقضاء الحاجة فاعتكافه باق

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو علي
rows.claim: Most grammarians, including al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, and Abū ʿAlī, take kāf as a noun meaning 'like,' governed by an omitted 'have you seen'; the preceding 'have you not seen' signals the omission.
rows.anchor: وإلى ذلك ذهب الكسائي والفراء وأبو علي وأكثر النحويين وحذف لدلالة ألم تر عليه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the kāf as extra, yielding a direct coordination with the earlier person who disputed Abraham.
rows.anchor: وإلى ذلك ذهب الأخفش أي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammarians analyze the coordination semantically, as though the text said 'Have you not seen the one who argued—or the one who passed?'; another view makes it Abraham challenging his opponent, which al-Ālūsī finds weak because of the distance and ellipsis.
rows.anchor: إنه عطف محمول على المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct coordination of the relative clause with the previous relative would require a preposition before kāf; as a noun it rarely accepts one, and as a particle it cannot.
rows.anchor: لم تجعل الكاف أصلية والعطف على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed distinction says 'have you not seen' introduces the object of wonder while 'have you seen' introduces its likeness; al-Ālūsī rejects it because both expressions occur with and without comparison in Arabic and Qurʾanic usage.
rows.anchor: يستعمل للتعجب مع التشبيه في كلام العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle aw marks a choice or a detailed alternative, and the passerby is most commonly identified as Ezra.
rows.anchor: والمار هو عزير بن شرخيا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ezra son of Sherekhya is reported from ʿAlī by al-Ḥākim and also from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, and numerous early authorities.
rows.anchor: كما أخرجه الحاكم عن علي كرم الله وجهه وإسحق بن بشر عن ابن عباس وعبدالله بن سلام

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Alternative identities are Armiya son of Ḥilqiyā, related by Abū Jaʿfar and favored by Wahb, or al-Khiḍr, related from Ibn Isḥāq; some say Armiya and al-Khiḍr are the same.
rows.anchor: هو أرميا بن خلقيا من بسط هرون عليه السلام وهو المروى عن أبي جعفر

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Other proposed identities include the prophet Shuʿayā and Lot's servant; Ibn Isḥāq is named for the al-Khiḍr identification.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو الخضر عليه السلام وحكى ذلك عن ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the passerby was an unbeliever in resurrection; he cites the narrative's parallel with Nimrod and the apparent wording of incredulity, but the author argues the surrounding context and the unusual event favor a believer instead.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : كان المار رجلا كافرا بالبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that the man's shared request to witness revival with Abraham and the extraordinary favor shown him make the unbeliever identification unlikely; his words can express wonder rather than denial.
rows.anchor: فإن كليهما طلبا معاينة الإحياء مع أن ما جرى له في القصة مما يبعد أن يجرى مع كافر

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: The village is identified by Ibn Zayd as the town from which thousands departed; other reports name Dayr Sāyir Abād, Dayr Salmābād, Dayr Hiraql, al-Muʾtafikah, or a grape-growing village near Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد : هى التى خرج منها الألوف

rows.speaker: عكرمة والربيع ووهب
rows.claim: ʿIkrimah, al-Rabīʿ, and Wahb identify the village as Jerusalem, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar; al-Ālūsī calls this the best-known view and derives qaryah from gathering.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة والربيع ووهب : هى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāwiyah ʿalā ʿurūshihā means either collapsed onto its roofs, with roofs falling first, or empty of inhabitants while its houses still stand; he rejects complicated grammatical accounts of the phrase.
rows.anchor: أي ساقطة على سقوفها بأن سقط السقف أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line 'he said' may describe speech inwardly or aloud; the demonstrative may point to the village itself, its inhabitants by ellipsis, or its decayed bones and corpses, with literal or figurative revival accordingly.
rows.anchor: المشار إليه إما نفس القرية بدون تقدير كما هو الظاهر فالإحياء والإماتة مجازان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the figurative reading, the passerby longs to see the ruined town rebuilt while sensing despair; on a literal reading, he either acknowledges his inability if a believer or denies the possibility if an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: فعلى القول بالمجاز يكون هذا القول على سبيل التلهف والتشوق إلى عمارة تلك القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers taking the village itself as the object of revival: the text describes the village rather than its people or bones, and omits any claim that the dead became dust or bones, which would intensify the impossibility.
rows.anchor: ورجح أول الاحتمالات الثلاثة في المشار إليه بأن إرادة إحياء لأهل أو عظامهم يأباه التعرض لحال القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted object receives emphasis because the wonder concerns the village, not the agent; annā means either 'when' as a temporal adverb or 'how' as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المفعول على الفاعل للاعتناء به من حيث إن الاستبعاد ناشئ من جهته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's causing him to die for a hundred years means keeping him dead for that duration, since the act of removing life does not itself extend over time; ʿām is linked etymologically to the sun's course.
rows.anchor: أي فألبثه ميتا مائة عام ولا بد من اعتبار هذا التضمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿath means raising him to life; it suggests swift, easy divine action and that he rose with his faculties intact, prepared to reflect.
rows.anchor: أي أحياه من بعثت الناقة إذا أقمتها من مكانها ولعل إيثاره على أحياه للدلالة على سرعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A narrative cited from al-Baḥr says that after his death God sent the Persian king Kusk with workers to rebuild Jerusalem; God destroyed Nebuchadnezzar with a mosquito, Israelites returned, and the restored city flourished before the passerby was revived.
rows.anchor: ففي البحر أنه لما مر له سبعون سنة من موته وقد منعه الله تعالى من السباع والطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question 'How long did you remain?' is introduced to expose the man's inability to grasp God's affairs and eliminate his doubts; kam is a temporal accusative with an omitted 'time' as its specification.
rows.anchor: ليظهر له العجز عن الإحاطة بشئون الله تعالى على أتم وجه وتنحسم مادة استبعاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent speaker is God, but other views name a heavenly voice, Gabriel, a prophet, or a believing witness who lived from the man's death to his revival; only the last makes attribution to God figurative.
rows.anchor: أن القائل هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man estimates that he remained a day or part of one, either by guess or because the interval seemed short; a report says he died in the morning and awoke before sunset, first saying a day then correcting himself after seeing the sun.
rows.anchor: قاله بناءا على التقريب والتخمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God corrects the estimate: he remained a hundred years, not a day or part of one.
rows.anchor: قال بل لبثت مائة عام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One opinion says his food was grapes or figs and his drink juice or milk.
rows.anchor: كان طعامه عنبا أو تينا وشرابه عصيرا أو لبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yatasannah means the food and drink did not change through the long period; its root is variously tied to the word for year or to clay that has become altered, while unchanged food means it stayed fresh.
rows.anchor: هذه المدة المتطاولة واشتقاقه من السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final letter is analyzed either as original hāʾ, as wāw with a pause hāʾ, or as a pause hāʾ after deletion; another account derives the form from lam yatasannan and explains consonant alteration.
rows.anchor: فقيل : هاء بدليل سانهت فلانا فهو مجزوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative clause is circumstantial; its pronoun refers either to food and drink collectively or only to the latter, whose unchanged state implies the former. ʿAbd Allāh and Ubay are cited for variant readings.
rows.anchor: واكتفى بدلالة حاله على حال الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative to look at the food may seem to follow from the hundred years, but al-Ālūsī says the man assumed little time because his body had not changed, making the food's preservation still more striking.
rows.anchor: بأن المفرع عليه ليس لبث المائة بل لبث المائة من غير تغير في جسمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says he was told to inspect quickly spoiling food as proof that God can resurrect; al-Ālūsī calls it strained and less consistent than the explicit mention of the donkey.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن التقدير إن حصل لك عدم طمأنينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The donkey was likely decomposed, with its bones weathered and joints separated; the claim that it remained alive without food or water is unsupported.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الظاهر لأنه أدل على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-li-najʿalaka is analyzed as a purpose adjunct to an omitted 'we did that,' or as attached to what precedes, with the conjunction treated as extra or as coordination; it means God acted to make him a sign for people.
rows.anchor: أي وفعلنا ذلك لنجعلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āyah means an instructive sign or guide; its audience may be humanity, the survivors of his people, or contemporaries who see a man from ancient generations and learn the lost Torah from him.
rows.anchor: أي عبرة أو مرشدا ﴿ للناس ﴾ أي جنسهم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies the bones as the donkey's; other reports say they are the dead villagers' or the passerby's own, with his eyes revived first while his body remained dead. Al-Ālūsī dismisses the competing accounts.
rows.anchor: أي عظام الحمار كما قاله السدي وكرر الأمر لما أن المأمور به أولا هو النظر إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With zāy, nunshizuhā means raising the bones from the earth and returning them to their places in the body; al-Kisāʾī glosses it as softening and enlarging them.
rows.anchor: بالزاى المعجمة من الانشاز وهو الرفع أي كيف نرفعها من الأرض فنردها إلى أماكنها

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubay reads nunshīhā; Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read nunshiruhā, understood as bringing the dead to life, though al-Ālūsī says life here may mean the prior stages because flesh follows.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي ننشيها وابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو ويعقوب ننشرها

rows.speaker: أبان عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abān from ʿĀṣim reads nunshiruhā with an alternative vocalization meaning to spread or unroll the bones, following al-Farrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان عن عاصم ننشرها بفتح النون وضم الشين والراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about how God raises the bones is parsed either as a circumstantial clause or as an explanatory apposition; although interrogative clauses normally resist circumstantial use, the question here is not literal.
rows.anchor: والجملة قيل : إما حال من العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage omits how the spirit is breathed into the body because explaining that process does not serve the relevant wisdom.
rows.anchor: ولعل عدم التعرض لكيفية نفخ الروح كما قيل لما أنها مما لا تقتضي الحكمة بيانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An account says an angel called the bones and they assembled from every direction; sinews, flesh, skin, and hair were restored, then spirit entered and the donkey rose braying toward heaven.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار إن ملكا نادى العظام فأجابت وأقبلت من كل ناحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When it became clear to him, he understood the stages of revival; the text omits the obvious assembling and clothing of the bones to emphasize its immediacy.
rows.anchor: للإيذان بظهور تحققه واستغنائه عن الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some treat tabayyana's implicit subject as governed jointly by tabayyana and aʿlam in a dispute over grammatical coordination; others read it as the event of clarity itself, supported by Ibn ʿAbbās's passive reading.
rows.anchor: فاعل تبين مضمر يفسره مفعول أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present form aʿlamu suggests continuing knowledge: the thing itself did not change, but its quality changed from inference to direct observation, showing his earlier words expressed ordinary astonishment rather than denial.
rows.anchor: وإيثار صبغة المضارع للدلالة على أن علمه بذلك مستمر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the phrase as an imperative, 'know'; Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly says Ezra was no better than Abraham, since God commanded each to know, and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī also read it as a command.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود قيل أعلم على وجه الأمر وأخرج سعيد بن منصور وابن المنذر عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If read as a command, its speaker may be God, the Prophet, an angel, or the man addressing and reproving himself for his prior astonishment.
rows.anchor: والآمر هو الله تعالى أو النبي أو الملك ويحتمل أن يكون المخاطب هو نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A post-revival story says Ezra rode home unrecognized, then found his former blind, disabled servant, now 120; she asked him to pray for restored sight, and he healed her eyes by prayer and touch before the segment breaks.
rows.anchor: فانطلق على وهم منهم حتى أتى منزله فإذا هو بعجوز عمياء مقعدة قد أتى عليها مائة وعشرون سنة
